digo_source: Pakia (2005) App. III, App. V, App. VI; Mgombato

teaser.en: Named after safari ants, though no one can quite say why.

summary.en: Mtsalafu is coffee senna, a common weed of farms and roadsides with yellow flowers and long thin pods. Its Digo name means 'safari ants', a link Pakia found no explanation for.

about.en: Mtsalafu is an upright, rank-smelling herb or soft shrub, usually waist-high, with leaves divided into four to six pairs of pointed leaflets. It bears bright yellow flowers followed by long, thin, flattened pods packed with seeds. The Digo recognise it by its leaves.

where.en: Originally from tropical America, it is now a widespread weed of cultivated land, compounds, roadsides and waste ground.

uses.en: Pakia records no Digo use. Elsewhere the roasted seeds have been used as a coffee substitute, hence its English name, but the raw seeds and plant are toxic to livestock.

culture.en: Pakia gives it as an example of a plant named after an animal for reasons no one could explain.

names.en: Pakia records the Digo name Mtsalafu and explains it as 'safari ants', though the connection between the plant and the ants is not clear. Mgombato confirms tsalafu as the safari ant. In English it is coffee senna or negro coffee; its scientific name is Senna occidentalis (formerly Cassia occidentalis).

reason.en: Also named after an animal for unclear reasons
